# REI pilot kit: usability and research reasoning

This is a provisional formative evaluation kit. It is not a validated test, and completing it does not establish research competence or a causal learning effect. Review the tasks and scoring with a research instructor before use. Follow your institution's requirements for collecting student evaluation data.

## What this pilot can answer

Can a student locate a useful source, distinguish a result from a causal claim, preserve a source-linked interpretation, select an appropriate kind of evidence, and return to saved work with little help? Separately: can the interface be operated without assistance?

## Preparation

Use students who have not already been taught the interface. Ask permission for observation. Explain that participation is voluntary, that the interface is being evaluated, and that they may stop. Use participant codes rather than names. Do not collect passwords, private participant datasets or unrelated personal information. Use the fictional CSV for analysis practice. Agree a retention and deletion plan for observations.

Record the REI release/date, browser/device, prior research experience and whether the student attended the workshop. Keep facilitator instructions consistent. A first round of five to eight students can expose usability problems; it is not a powered effectiveness study or a representative sample. Ask an instructor to examine the academic reasoning as well as the clicks.

## Suggested 35-minute session

1. Independent baseline task, 5 minutes. Give Form A below before demonstrating REI. Keep answers separate from the website.
2. Explore the whole-project example, 5 minutes. Ask the student to explain which parts are published evidence and which parts are proposed. Do not lead them to the answer.
3. Real-paper task, 8 minutes. Find the interview study in Learn, locate a method or limitation in its original PDF, save it to a clearly named practice project, and record a source-linked interpretation. Observe navigation, assistance and source/page accuracy.
4. Data task, 5 minutes. In Create, load the fictional CSV, describe study_minutes, inspect its relationship with quiz_score and explain missing row 7. Ask whether the output establishes an intervention effect.
5. Independent transfer task, 5 minutes. Use Form B without the worked answer visible.
6. Return and handoff task, 5 minutes. Reload, locate saved work, download a complete project handoff with a next-step note, and identify how the recipient would restore it. Do not delete valuable work during the pilot.
7. Short interview, 2 minutes. Ask what was useful, what was confusing, what they would otherwise have used, and whether any task felt like unnecessary copying.

## Parallel reasoning forms

Form A:

- A voluntary, one-time student survey finds that study-app users report more study time. What can you conclude, what can you not conclude, and what details would you inspect?
- You want to understand how commuting students manage study. You can interview people with relevant experience. Propose a bounded question and explain the fit between question, evidence and analysis.
- A search returns very few relevant papers. Explain one justified revision and how you would check whether it helped.

Form B:

- A voluntary, one-time survey finds that students who attend a study club report higher confidence. What can you conclude, what can you not conclude, and what details would you inspect?
- You want to understand how students working part-time manage course communication. You can interview people with relevant experience. Propose a bounded question and explain the fit between question, evidence and analysis.
- A search returns many weakly relevant papers. Explain one justified revision and how you would check whether it helped.

These forms are intended to probe related skills; their difficulty has not been equated. Counterbalance their order where practical. A pre/post difference can reflect practice, facilitator help or unequal form difficulty and does not by itself demonstrate REI caused an improvement.

## Provisional instructor rubric

Rate each dimension separately as 0 (absent/incorrect), 1 (partially justified) or 2 (accurate and explicitly justified). Record the actual response and a reason for the judgment. These anchors require instructor calibration; do not automatically award points for key words.

- Claim boundaries: distinguishes association from cause and bounds the population/setting.
- Evidence fit: identifies evidence and analysis that can address the stated aim.
- Source interpretation: accurately represents the original passage, with a correct source and location.
- Search reasoning: explains a defensible revision and a way to inspect its consequences.
- Uncertainty: identifies a relevant limitation or missing detail and explains why it matters.

For the source task, the instructor must check the original paper, not just whether fields contain text. Have two reviewers independently score a subset and discuss disagreements before using a common rubric. Do not call these scores a validated mastery scale or compare students for high-stakes decisions.

## Usability observations

For each task record: completed independently / completed with assistance / incomplete; the concrete mistake; assistance supplied; source or data error; and whether the student could explain the result. Time is useful context, not a quality score. Note device and accessibility barriers. Avoid collecting background browsing activity.

Use REI-pilot-observations.csv as a blank record. Keep reasoning and usability outcomes separate. A student can navigate quickly and reason incorrectly, or reason well while struggling with the interface.

## Delayed follow-up

If students consent and your setting permits it, ask them about one new source or question about a week later, with no model answer open. Assess transfer using the same dimensions. Arrange any contact yourself; REI has no automatic messaging or study scheduler.

## Decision after the pilot

List repeated breakdowns and prioritize their effect on learning or task completion. Revise confusing prompts and incorrect interpretations before expanding content. A small observed pilot supports product refinement. Establishing educational effectiveness would require a suitable study design, ethical/institutional review where applicable, an appropriate comparison, defensible measures and adequate analysis.

## Guidance informing the design

- IES practice guide on worked examples, retrieval and explanatory questions: https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1
- ACRL information-literacy framework: https://www.ala.org/acrl/standards/ilframework
- NIST guidance on exploratory data analysis: https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/eda.htm

These sources inform instructional and analytic choices. None validates REI or this pilot instrument.
